sentences.text: The holotype fossil consists only of the front part of a snout.
In side view, the snout is rounded, it bears no crest, and the palate curves upwards.
The first pair of teeth sits at the tip, which is flat and wider than it is tall when viewed from the front.
The second and third pairs of teeth are obliquely pointed sideways.
C. nasutus displays a unique dental density of three teeth per three centimeters at the front of the jaw and 2.5 teeth at the rear.

A unique combination of traits includes a straight or slightly curved upper snout profile, a palate midline extending to the back of the second tooth pair, gradually increasing tooth spacing posteriorly, obliquely pointing second and third tooth pairs, and a slightly expanded snout front.
Harry Govier Seeley originally named the species Ptenodactylus nasutus in 1869 based on fossils from Haslingfield, Cambridgeshire.
Richard Owen named Pterodactylus sedgwickii in 1859 based on the front part of a snout from the Cambridge Greensand.
Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner established the genus Camposipterus in 2013 after determining the species was distinct from Anhanguera fittoni.
The genus name honors Brazilian paleontologist Diogenes de Almeida Campos and the Greek word for wing.
The holotype specimen was found in the Cambridge Greensand, which dates to the Cenomanian but likely contains older Albian fossils.
In 2013, Rodrigues and Kellner transferred two additional species into the genus Camposipterus.
The question mark in the species names indicates that the authors were not certain about the validity of transferring those species to the genus.
Seeley speculated that a depression on the snout might serve for lip attachment, but pterosaurs instead had horny coverings.
Rodrigues and Kellner assigned Camposipterus to the clade Anhangueria but placed it incertae sedis due to an unknown position.
A 2019 study by Jacobs et al. placed Camposipterus within the family Ornithocheiridae as the sister taxon of Cimoliopterus.
Camposipterus(?) sedgwickii was reassigned to the genus Aerodraco in 2020.
Rodrigues and Kellner treated Camposipterus as a clade defined by a unique combination of traits rather than a single shared derived character.
Rodrigues and Kellner assigned Camposipterus to the clade Anhangueria but placed it as an incertae sedis, meaning its exact position is uncertain.
Some cladistic analyses suggested Camposipterus was more derived than Cimoliopterus but less derived than Cearadactylus atrox.
Camposipterus lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 112 million years ago.
Camposipterus lived during the Albian stage, from 106.3 to 100.5 million years ago.
Camposipterus was a pterodactyloid pterosaur found in England.
Camposipterus belongs to the parent group Anhangueria.
Camposipterus is classified as a reptile.
There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Camposipterus in the Paleobiology Database.
Researchers express uncertainty regarding the validity of assigning certain species to the genus Camposipterus.
In 2025, Pêgas assigned O. colorhinus to the genus Cimoliopterus based on its close relationship to C. cuvieri.
